analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to affirmatively approve every major federal regulation before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: With 85 Republican cosponsors, the bill died in the House Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the law as it stands, a major federal rule takes effect unless Congress passes a law to stop it — and that has almost never happened. This bill would flip the default: any rule costing the economy $100 million or more could not take effect unless both the House and Senate passed, and the President signed, a resolution approving it within 90 days. If Congress did nothing, the rule would die automatically. Supporters said this makes unelected regulators accountable to elected officials; the practical effect would be that hundreds of major rules each year — on workplace safety, clean air, food safety, financial practices — would likely never take effect because of congressional gridlock.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be regulated businesses — manufacturers, energy companies, financial firms, and others facing costly federal rules — because a rule costing $100 million or more would simply die unless Congress affirmatively approved it, which in practice it rarely would. Supporters also argued citizens would gain accountability, since rules would need approval from elected representatives rather than career agency staff.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated businesses facing costly federal rules

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require a joint resolution of approval, enacted into law, before any major rule could take effect, addressing the argument that rules costing the economy $100 million or more should be decided by elected officials rather than agency staff [S2] [S3].

It would flip the current default: instead of rules taking effect unless Congress votes to reject them, rules would be deemed not approved if Congress did not act within 90 session or legislative days [S2] [S3].

It preserved narrow escape valves: a major rule could take effect for one 90-day stretch if the President found an imminent threat to health or safety, a need to enforce criminal laws, a national security need, or a trade-agreement obligation, and monetary policy rules were exempted entirely [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The people who rely on federal safeguards would bear the cost: workers counting on safety rules, communities relying on clean-air and clean-water rules, and consumers protected by financial and product rules. Because the bill required an affirmative vote by both chambers within 90 days for every major rule, congressional inaction alone would kill those rules — and with thousands of rules finalized each year (3,006 in 2008, of which 94 were major, per the bill's own findings), most would never get a vote.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers, consumers, and communities relying on federal safeguards

drawbacks.text: The bill's own design makes congressional gridlock a standing veto: a major rule is 'deemed not to be approved' and cannot take effect if Congress fails to act within 90 days, so a single chamber's silence would kill workplace, environmental, and financial protections without anyone voting on them [S2] [S3].

Only a narrow category of rules — emergencies, criminal-law enforcement, national security, trade-agreement rules, and monetary policy — could temporarily take effect without approval, leaving most protective rules exposed to dying by inaction [S2] [S3].

An honest supporter would have to acknowledge the trade-off: the bill addresses the real concern that unelected officials write binding rules with large costs, but the remedy shifts that power not to careful deliberation but to congressional inaction, which systematically favors whatever regulated industry wants the rule blocked.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a genuine structural question — Congress delegates lawmaking to agencies, and the public cannot vote regulators out. But its remedy was blunt: by making approval mandatory and inaction fatal, it would have effectively let any well-positioned industry stall a major rule until it died. For ordinary people, the likely result was fewer safeguards, not more accountability, and the drawbacks outweighed the accountability benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, passed along to a subcommittee, and never brought up for a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 8, 2009 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, with additional referral to the House Rules Committee [S1] [S5].
On October 19, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, the usual parking place for bills leadership does not intend to move [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].
It had substantial backing on paper: 85 House Republicans signed on as cosponsors, and the original sponsors included the top House Republican leaders of the day [S3] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal agencies kept the existing process — rules take effect unless Congress affirmatively disapproves them — and the people covered by those rules, including workers and communities relying on safety and environmental protections, kept safeguards that would have been at risk. The bill's backers gained nothing. The idea resurfaced in later Congresses with House Republican majorities, where versions of it passed the House.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on existing federal protections

for.name: Rep. Geoff Davis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require congressional approval of major rules before they take effect.

for.name: 85 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it.

for.name: House Republican leaders including Rep. John Boehner and Rep. Eric Cantor
for.role: Minority Leader and Minority Whip (original cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, signaling leadership support for the bill.

against.name: Rep. John Conyers
against.what_they_did: Presided over the committee that received the bill, referred it to a subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or committee vote.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from October 2009 until the Congress ended in January 2011 without any action after its subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 85 cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill; the Democratic majority that controlled the House committees never allowed it a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have let any major rule — defined as one costing the economy $100 million or more — die unless both chambers approved it, giving regulated industries a powerful tool to block costly safety, environmental, and financial rules through congressional inaction. The savings to industry would come directly out of protections for workers, consumers, and communities.
Agencies would lose their power to issue binding major rules on their own; every rule with $100 million or more in economic impact would need an enacted law of Congress to take effect.
